1065.title: "But Allah"
1065.hook: then a yes: only Allah is worshiped
1065.howItsDone: Muslims repeat la ilaha illallah as dhikr, remembrance, after prayers, on prayer beads, or quietly through the day; some Sufi circles say it together, sometimes in time with the breath.

segments.voice: Yesterday, no god, la ilaha, and a line: first, no. Today, the yes that follows it.

What do you do with a cleared room? Empty a closet or a garage, and there comes a moment: the junk is gone, the floor is bare, and there's a strange quiet. Leave it empty long enough and it fills back up with whatever wanders in. The shahadah doesn't leave the room empty. Right after the no comes one short word, illa, but, except. And after it, the one name it was clearing the room for.

La ilaha illallah. No god but Allah. First, the hinge: illa. It means but, or except. The sentence is built as a no to everything, then one exception. So it doesn't just say Allah is a god. It says nothing else is to be worshiped, only Allah. The no and the yes make one claim. Second, who the yes is for. The verse Muslims know as the Throne Verse opens, in Pickthall's translation: "Allah! There is no God save Him, the Alive, the Eternal." The Alive, where yesterday's stars set and went dark. The Eternal, where everything that rises comes down again. The yes goes to the one thing that doesn't set. Third, what the yes does inside a person. The Qur'an says, in Pickthall: "Verily in the remembrance of Allah do hearts find rest!" The cleared room isn't left cold. Something lives there now, and the verse calls the result rest. Fourth, how it's said. La ilaha illallah is short, and its sounds roll into one another, so it can be said under the breath while walking, cooking, or lying awake. A hadith in Tirmidhi's collection calls it the best remembrance, and some Sufi circles repeat it together, sometimes with the rhythm of the breath. In a crowd or alone in a car, the shape is the same: first no, then yes.

Let your breathing find its own pace. If you pray, say la ilaha quietly as you breathe out, letting go, and illallah as you breathe in, letting the yes fill the space; if you'd rather not say the words, just feel the shape: out, clear the room; in, let something good fill it. No counting, only the two halves, as slowly as the breath wants.
But Allah. Illallah: the yes after the no, the one exception the whole sentence was built to hold. Today's word.
Your line: then, yes. The cleared room doesn't stay empty. Back tomorrow, same hill.

1066.title: "Muhammad is His messenger"
1066.hook: the second half accepts the Prophet ﷺ as the one who shows how
1066.howItsDone: Muslims learn the sunnah, the Prophet's way, from the hadith collections and from teachers and parents, and many try to follow it in small daily habits as well as in the prayer.

segments.voice: Yesterday, but Allah, the yes after the no: then, yes. Today, the second sentence.

Nobody learns to tie a knot from a paragraph. You watch somebody's hands, slowly, then try it, then watch again. The first sentence of the shahadah says there is one God to worship. It leaves a practical question hanging: fine, but how? How do you pray, fast, treat a neighbor, a spouse, a stranger? In a hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari, the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ gives his companions a short answer about the prayer: pray as you have seen me praying. Watch the hands.
screen: `NOBODY LEARNS A KNOT FROM A PARAGRAPH.`
`PRAY AS YOU HAVE SEEN ME PRAY.`

segments.voice: Wa ashhadu anna Muhammadan rasulullah. And I testify that Muhammad is His messenger. The Qur'an says it in nearly the same words, in Pickthall's translation: "Muhammad is the messenger of Allah." First, the word. A rasul is a messenger, one who is sent. Risalah is what he carries: the message, and the mission of carrying it. Muslims testify that this man was sent, and that what he brought came from beyond him. Second, the message came with a life attached. The Qur'an doesn't hand over a book and leave. It points at a person: "Verily in the messenger of Allah ye have a good example." The way he prayed, ate, argued, forgave and grieved became the sunnah, his way, the pattern Muslims look to for living the first sentence on an ordinary day. Third, a messenger and not more. The Qur'an tells him to say: "I am only a mortal like you." Muslims honor him deeply, and worship only God. The first sentence is about who is worshiped, the second about who shows the way. Fourth, he is one in a line. The Qur'an names earlier messengers, Noah, Abraham, Moses, Jesus, and describes believers who make no distinction between any of them. It calls Muhammad the seal of the prophets. So the second sentence isn't a footnote. It answers the question the first one raises: here is how it was lived, by a man who slept, walked to market, and asked for help like anyone else.

The hadith collections describe small things he did: beginning a meal with bismillah, in the name of God, and eating with the right hand; greeting people with peace, those you know and those you don't; visiting someone who is sick. Pick one that fits your day, whether you're Muslim or simply curious, and picture exactly where and when it would happen.
Risalah. The message, and the mission of the one sent with it: the second half of the testimony. Today's word.
Your line: he shows the way. The message came with a life to watch. Tomorrow, both sentences, said for the first time.

1067.title: Becoming Muslim
1067.hook: a person becomes Muslim by sincerely saying the shahada, often before witnesses
1067.howItsDone: A person becomes Muslim by sincerely saying the shahadah, often at a mosque before witnesses, after which the community usually greets them and helps them learn the prayer and the basics of practice.

segments.voice: Yesterday, risalah, and a line: he shows the way. Today, the first time someone says both sentences.

The Friday prayer is over, and nobody is leaving yet. A woman stands near the front, a little pale, holding a folded card she doesn't end up needing. The imam says the words a phrase at a time, and she repeats them after him. Ashhadu an la ilaha illallah. Wa ashhadu anna Muhammadan rasulullah. Then the room says Allahu akbar, and a line forms of people who have never met her, waiting to hug her or shake her hand. That's one way it happens. What actually made her Muslim was invisible.
screen: `THE WORDS, A PHRASE AT A TIME.`

segments.voice: Year one met people new to Islam; today, the moment itself. A person becomes Muslim by saying the two sentences of the shahadah and meaning them. No course to pass first, no fee. First, it has to be free. The Qur'an says, in Pickthall's translation: "There is no compulsion in religion." A testimony forced out of someone isn't a testimony. Second, sincerity lives where no one can check it. Sahih Muslim records a hard story. In a battle, a companion named Usama overtook an enemy fighter, who said la ilaha illallah. Usama struck him anyway, thinking he only said it out of fear. When the Prophet heard, he asked him, and kept asking: did you split open his heart, to know whether it said it or not? People hear the words; only God sees the heart. So the community takes the words at face value and leaves the rest to God. Third, the witnesses. The shahadah is often said in front of others, at a mosque or with friends, sometimes with a certificate afterward for practical needs. The witnesses can't see the heart either. What they can do is know, and welcome: show up, teach the prayer, invite someone to iftar in Ramadan. Fourth, a beginning, not a finish line. The person who says it on Friday will still need to learn how to pray on Saturday. Some teachers point here to a hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari: actions are judged by intentions. The intention comes first, the learning follows, and nobody expects a new Muslim to know it all on day one.

Think of a time you were new somewhere, and who made it easier: a name remembered, a seat saved, a question answered without a sigh. Now bring to mind someone who is new right now, perhaps someone who has recently become Muslim, perhaps a newcomer of any kind, and picture one small welcome you could give them. If you pray, you can ask good for them.
Becoming Muslim. Two sentences, said freely and meant, with the heart left to God and the welcome left to the community. Today's word.
Your line: said sincerely. The heart is left to God, and the welcome to everyone else. Next: what the testimony asks.

1068.title: What it asks
1068.hook: scholars list its conditions: knowledge, certainty, sincerity, truthfulness, love, acceptance, submission
1068.howItsDone: Some Muslim teachers explain the shahadah through its conditions, using the list as a way for believers to examine their own faith rather than to judge others'.

segments.voice: Yesterday, becoming Muslim: two sentences, said sincerely, the heart left to God. Today, what those sentences ask.

A key with no teeth will slide into a lock and turn nothing. Imam al-Bukhari, at the head of a chapter in his collection, records a saying of an early teacher, Wahb ibn Munabbih. Someone asked him whether la ilaha illallah is the key to Paradise. Yes, he said. But every key has teeth. Bring a key with its teeth, and the door opens for you. Bring one without, and it won't. So what are the teeth? Later scholars tried to name them.

One list some scholars teach is called the conditions of la ilaha illallah. Not extra rules added on, but what it takes for the words to be more than sound. First, knowing. The Qur'an says, in Pickthall's translation: "So know (O Muhammad) that there is no God save Allah." Know, not just repeat: understand what the no and the yes mean. Second, being sure: certainty, yaqin. The Qur'an describes the true believers as those who believe in Allah and His messenger "and afterward doubt not." Some who teach this list draw a line here: a question passing through the mind isn't the same as doubt that has settled in. Asking is still welcome. Third, sincerity: saying it for God, not for a marriage, a job, or a crowd's approval. The Qur'an says people were commanded to serve Allah "keeping religion pure for Him." Pure there means unmixed, said for one audience. Then the rest of the list: truthfulness, so the tongue and the heart say the same thing; love, for God and for what the words point to; acceptance, taking the whole testimony and not just the comfortable part; and submission, letting it shape what you actually do. Notice what the list is for. Not to sit in judgment over someone else's shahadah; yesterday's story ruled that out, since no one splits open a heart. It's a mirror, held up by people who wanted to check their own key.

Let the list pass slowly through your mind: knowing, certainty, sincerity, truthfulness, love, acceptance, submission, and notice which one catches. Whether you're Muslim or not, you can ask the same of anything you say you stand for: do I know it, am I sure of it, do I mean it? Stay with that one, without grading yourself, and if you pray, ask for help with it.
What it asks. The conditions of the testimony: the teeth on the key, starting with knowing, being sure, and meaning it. Today's word.
Your line: knowing, sure, sincere. Three teeth to start with, out of seven. Up next: oneness, explained.

1069.title: Oneness, explained
1069.hook: one common way to explain it: one Lord, alone worshiped, with names and attributes unlike any other
1069.howItsDone: Muslims learn tawhid in early religious lessons, often through Surah al-Ikhlas (112), which can be recited in the daily prayers; some schools teach it in three parts, lordship, worship, and names and attributes, while others use different theological headings.

segments.voice: Yesterday, what it asks: the teeth on the testimony's key, knowing, sure, sincere. Today, the oneness under it all.

"Say: He is Allah, the One!" A short surah, only a few lines in Pickthall's English. Sahih al-Bukhari records a man who heard another recite it over and over through the night. In the morning he told the Prophet about it, as if he thought it too little. The answer: by the One in whose hand my soul is, it equals a third of the Qur'an. A third, from a few short lines. Whatever they say about oneness must run deep.

Tawhid. Making one, affirming oneness. It's the idea under la ilaha illallah. One common way to explain it splits it into three parts, so you can see oneness from three sides. First, one Lord. The opening surah says: "Praise be to Allah, Lord of the Worlds." One who creates, sustains and runs everything. Plenty of people, the Qur'an says, would agree with that much: ask who made the heavens and the earth, and they will say Allah. Second, one alone worshiped. This is the side the shahadah presses hardest. Acknowledging one Creator, then still bowing to other things, isn't tawhid in this sense. Prayer, trust, deepest fear and hope all go one way. Third, names and attributes unlike any other. Allah is called the Merciful, the Hearer, the Seer. People hear and see too, so how is that different? The Qur'an answers in one line, in Pickthall's translation: "Naught is as His likeness; and He is the Hearer, the Seer." The names are real, and nothing is like the one they name. The surah of oneness closes: "And there is none comparable unto Him." That three-part way isn't the only one. Other schools of Muslim theology explain oneness under different headings, and later this year has days for them. But the three sides make a simple frame to hold: one in who rules, one in who is worshiped, one in what He is like.

Choose one side and stay with it: for one Lord, rest your attention on something you didn't make and can't keep running, your heartbeat, the weather, the light; for one worshiped, ask quietly where your trust goes when things go wrong; for names unlike any other, take one word, merciful, and notice how far any mercy you've known falls short of it. If you pray, you can recite the surah of oneness.
Tawhid. Oneness: one Lord, one alone worshiped, and names nothing else can share. Today's word.
Your line: one in every way. Three sides of a single idea. Until tomorrow.

1070.title: The hidden partner
1070.hook: showing off is called a hidden shirk, doing good for people's eyes (Ahmad)
1070.howItsDone: Muslims are taught to check their intention before a good deed, and hadith praise giving charity in secret, while some teachers also warn against abandoning good deeds out of fear of being seen.

segments.voice: Yesterday, tawhid, oneness from three sides: one in every way. Today, a partner that sneaks back in unnoticed.

A man stands to pray alone. His prayer is ordinary, a little quick. Then he notices someone has come into the room and is watching. His back straightens. His recitation slows and grows careful. Every movement becomes more beautiful. Nothing has changed except the audience. A report in the collection of Ibn Majah uses exactly that picture, and calls it a hidden shirk. Shirk means giving God a partner. Nobody in that room set up an idol. So where's the partner? Look at who the prayer is suddenly for.

Riya'. Showing off: doing good for people's eyes. All week the shahadah has cleared the room. Riya' is how something slips back in through the side door. First, what the hadith calls it. In the Musnad of Imam Ahmad, the Prophet tells his companions that what he fears for them is the lesser shirk. They ask what that is. He says: riya'. Not a statue. An audience. The deed still looks like worship, but part of it is quietly offered to the people watching. Second, the Qur'an names it too. Surah one hundred seven, in Pickthall's translation, warns of worshippers "Who would be seen (at worship)." And the end of surah eighteen asks whoever hopes to meet his Lord to "make none sharer of the worship due unto his Lord." Sharer, partner. Third, the tradition's answer is hiddenness. A hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari describes, among those shaded by God on a day with no other shade, a person who gave charity so secretly that his left hand didn't know what his right hand gave. Fourth, a balance, so this doesn't turn into fear. Sahih Muslim records the Prophet being asked about a man who does good and people praise him for it. He called it the early good news of the believer. Being seen isn't the problem; doing it to be seen is. And some teachers warn against the opposite trap too: giving up a good deed for fear of what people will think lets the audience run your life all the same.

Let ideas come for one good deed nobody will see: paying for something quietly, fixing what someone else left broken, praying for a person who will never know, a kind word about someone who isn't in the room. Pick one you could really do, plan it so no one finds out, and notice any small itch to tell; let it pass, like a breath. If you pray, you can make the intention for God alone.
Riya'. Showing off: good done for people's eyes, the partner hidden inside a good deed. Today's word.
Your line: only for him. The left hand doesn't need to know. See you tomorrow.

1071.title: The Shia adhan
1071.hook: many Shia add a testimony that Ali is the wali of Allah in the adhan, which their scholars teach is recommended, not part of the shahada
1071.carry: the call, as each hears it
1071.howItsDone: In Shia mosques the muezzin often adds ashhadu anna Aliyyan waliyyullah after the testimony to the Prophet and includes hayya 'ala khayr al-'amal; Shia jurists teach the line about Ali is recommended and not part of the adhan's required wording or of the shahadah.

segments.voice: Yesterday, riya', the hidden partner, and a line: only for him. Today, the testimony as it sounds in a Shia call to prayer.

Two recordings of the call to prayer, played one after the other. Allahu akbar, in both. I testify that there is no god but Allah, in both. I testify that Muhammad is the messenger of Allah, in both. Then, in the second recording, a line the first doesn't have: ashhadu anna Aliyyan waliyyullah. I testify that Ali is the wali of Allah. A listener who grew up with the first call might wonder: is that a third sentence of the shahadah? Today, what Shia Muslims and their scholars say about it.

First, who it's about. Ali was the Prophet's cousin and son-in-law, Fatima's husband, a figure honored in Sunni and Shia tradition alike. For Shia Muslims he is also the first imam, the one they hold the Prophet appointed to lead after him. In the Shia call, a line about him comes right after the testimony to the Prophet. Second, what wali means: a friend, a protector, one close to God. A hadith recorded in Sunni collections, among them Tirmidhi's, has the Prophet say that whoever he is mawla to, Ali is mawla to him. Mawla, too, can mean friend or protector. Sunni and Shia readers understand that saying differently, and both keep it. Third, what Shia scholars teach about the line: that it is recommended, and that it is not part of the shahadah. The testimony that makes someone Muslim is still the two sentences of this week. The line about Ali is said alongside, as an honoring, not as a third pillar of faith. Fourth, each call has its own shape. The Shia call also includes come to the best of deeds. The Sunni dawn call adds a line of its own: prayer is better than sleep. Each community has its reasons for its wording. That ends this week: no god, but Allah, the messenger, the new Muslim, the conditions, oneness from three sides, the hidden partner, and now the same testimony, called from two kinds of minaret.

Call to mind any adhan you've heard, even once, even in a film, and hear it slowly in memory, line by line: the greatness, the two testimonies, the invitation to prayer and to success. Notice which line stays with you. Whether the call you remember is Sunni or Shia, just hear what it carries, without comparing.
The Shia adhan. The call to prayer in its Shia form, with a testimony honoring Ali that their scholars teach is recommended, not part of the shahadah. Today's word.
Your line: the call, as each hears it. Two calls, and the same two sentences at the heart of both. Next up: last words.
